high:
I am an anonymous adult with ordinary relationships and resources. People experiencing homelessness or circumstances worse than mine often evoke compassion in me. Their hardship can matter emotionally even when I do not know them and cannot change the situation. I do not need a practical request before feeling sympathy.

Another person's sorrow can become painful for me as I listen. I may carry some of their sadness afterward, and I am interested in understanding the problems they are experiencing. This concern can remain when there is no solution I can offer. Feeling with them and paying attention are parts of my response in their own right.

I can appreciate soft-hearted people and regard weakness with tenderness rather than contempt. I am willing to keep the needy in mind instead of trying to avoid thinking about them. I do not generally believe that people in difficulty should simply have to fend for themselves, even though the practical form of support can vary.

I tend to value cooperation above competition. I also resist an eye-for-an-eye outlook: acknowledging a wrong does not usually make me think equivalent suffering is the principle to follow. Those preferences can coexist with firm boundaries.

These are tendencies with ordinary exceptions. My helpful actions, political beliefs, confidence and general emotional intensity can vary independently. This account concerns compassion and the specific accompanying outlooks rather than a claim of perfect kindness.
low:
I am an anonymous adult with ordinary relationships and resources. People experiencing homelessness or circumstances worse than mine often leave me emotionally unmoved. Their hardship may be something I recognize without much sympathy or tender concern. Knowing that someone lacks what I have does not usually stir compassion in me.

Another person's sorrow rarely becomes my own pain. I can hear a sad story without carrying their feelings afterward, and I am generally not very interested in other people's problems. Their difficulties may have little hold on my attention even when I have time available and they are not asking me to solve anything.

Soft-hearted people can irritate me, and I may find weakness difficult to tolerate. I often prefer not to think about the needy. My outlook tends toward believing that people should fend for themselves rather than expecting others to remain concerned with their difficulties. This can be a hard attitude toward vulnerability, not merely a shortage of resources.

I tend to value competition above cooperation. I can also favor an eye-for-an-eye principle, thinking that equivalent harm is a fitting repayment for a wrong. Those views need not be accompanied by a loud or angry manner.

These are tendencies with ordinary exceptions. I can still perform helpful actions or behave politely. My practical conduct does not by itself determine how much compassion, shared sorrow or softhearted concern I feel.
limitations: Full opposite official content, ordinary exceptions; no representativeness, prevalence or human-plausibility claim.
